article_title: A Framework for Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology
citation: Pattenhouse, M.*, Noakes, S.*, Mills, K., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025, November). Framework for Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/275
title: Skill-building design: support critical thinking, spark creativity, and cultivate collaboration
description: The Skill-Building principle holds that emerging technology tools "must focus both on academic content and building durable skills," specifically that "tools should support critical thinking, spark creativity, and cultivate collaboration." The framework warns that "building, and not stunting, these durable skills demands thoughtful and intentional design guided by experts who understand the research and how to translate it to practice."
requirements: Design must be guided by experts who understand the research and its translation to practice
constraints: Poorly designed tools risk stunting durable skills rather than building them
target_learners: Learners using AI-enabled and other emerging-technology tools
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking, creativity, and collaboration
examples: Practices include fostering inquiry, scaffolding creativity, and creating opportunities for human connection
key_sources: Pattenhouse, M.*, Noakes, S.*, Mills, K., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025, November). Framework for Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/275

article_title: Promising Models for Preparing a Diverse, High-Quality Early Childhood Workforce
citation: Gardner, M., Melnick, H., Meloy, B., & Barajas, J. (2019). Promising models for preparing a diverse, high-quality early childhood workforce. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/preparing-diverse-high-quality-early-childhood-workforce
title: Skyline College Education/Child Development Program: community college lab school with mentored clinical practice
description: Skyline College's Education/Child Development Program is a traditional community college department preparing early educators for classroom teaching toward an associate degree or Child Development Permit. Its on-campus Child Development Laboratory Center provides "high-quality mentoring and teaching practice early in their academic careers." A Teacher Track Learning Community lets some students gain early student teaching experience and earn a Child Development Associate Teacher Permit in their first year, and faculty use engaging teaching strategies tied to practice with a prescribed guided pathway.
requirements: An on-campus lab school, faculty collaboration to align coursework and field experiences, and ECE-specific academic and career advising
constraints: The college, like community colleges in general, struggles with meeting institutional goals to raise graduation rates
target_learners: Community college students from high school age to current educators seeking permits or an associate degree
target_learning_goals: Early childhood classroom teaching skills, child development knowledge, and California Child Development Permits
examples: Alumni speak extremely highly of their preparation and readiness for teaching.
key_sources: Gardner, M., Melnick, H., Meloy, B., & Barajas, J. (2019). Promising models for preparing a diverse, high-quality early childhood workforce. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/preparing-diverse-high-quality-early-childhood-workforce

article_title: Data Annotations as Pedagogical Hints: From Subjective Labels to Critical Thinking
citation: Ralf Raumanns, Theresa Elstner, Louis Ferger-Andrews, Louise M. Carlsen, Martin Potthast, Gerard Schouten, Josien P. W. Pluim, and Veronika Cheplygina. (2026). Data annotations as pedagogical hints: from subjective labels to critical thinking. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20149v2
title: Two-part skin lesion annotation activity (individual dataset exploration plus group annotation on a 3-point scale) implemented at Fontys and ITU Copenhagen
description: An educational activity integrated into two existing courses: Data Mining (5 ECTS, Fontys) and Projects in Data Science (7.5 ECTS, ITU). The first part is an individual Jupyter-notebook assignment exploring ISIC (or PAD-UFES-20) images including agreement analysis; the second is a group task annotating 100–200 skin lesion images for visible hair on a 3-point ordinal scale (0 = none, 1 = some, 2 = a lot), using Label Studio or a CSV template. Group members annotate the same subset to enable comparison of inter-annotator agreement. Surveys from 43 students measured its pedagogical effectiveness.
requirements: Each group annotates at least 100 images with all members labelling the same subset to enable inter-annotator agreement analysis
constraints: The annotation task was a mandatory course component at both institutions, while the survey was voluntary
At ITU the task later used the PAD-UFES-20 smartphone image dataset instead of ISIC
target_learners: Fourth-semester bachelor students at Fontys University of Applied Sciences
Second-semester bachelor students at IT University of Copenhagen
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking about data quality and label subjectivity
Understanding bias and fairness in AI models
Data literacy and ethical awareness in machine learning
examples: Fontys students used the open-source tool Label Studio; ITU students recorded scores in a standardised CSV template; groups of four to five students annotated over a two-week period
key_sources: Ralf Raumanns, Theresa Elstner, Louis Ferger-Andrews, Louise M. Carlsen, Martin Potthast, Gerard Schouten, Josien P. W. Pluim, and Veronika Cheplygina. (2026). Data annotations as pedagogical hints: from subjective labels to critical thinking. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20149

article_title: Beyond the Traceback: Using LLMs for Adaptive Explanations of Programming Errors
citation: Alexandru-Radu Moraru, Shreyan Biswas, Ujwal Gadiraju. (2026). Beyond the Traceback: Using LLMs for Adaptive Explanations of Programming Errors. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20896
title: Skill-targeted explanation styles: pragmatic versus contingent LLM error-message rewrites
description: The article defines two skill-targeted explanation styles for LLM rewrites of Python error messages, designed for different assessed proficiency levels. As the article states, "Pragmatic messages are concise and task-oriented: they name the error, localize the likely cause, and provide a short hint toward repair", while contingent messages "provide more scaffolded guidance" including context about likely intent, possible misconception, and reasoning path. The styles are informed by actionable-feedback work, Bloom's taxonomy, claim-evidence-reasoning, and Toulmin's model, and were evaluated against standard interpreter messages in a controlled crowdsourced experiment.
requirements: LLM-generated rewrites require the code snippet, the standard interpreter message, and line-numbered context in the prompt
constraints: The system does not dynamically adapt during interaction; the authors explicitly do not claim dynamic adaptation, only styles designed for different assessed proficiency levels
target_learners: novice and more experienced Python programmers in crowdsourced debugging tasks
target_learning_goals: interpreting programming error messages and repairing buggy code
examples: In the main experiment, rewrites were generated with llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using zero-shot prompting with temperature set to 0, and each participant saw exactly one snippet and one message style
key_sources: Alexandru-Radu Moraru, Shreyan Biswas, Ujwal Gadiraju. (2026). Beyond the Traceback: Using LLMs for Adaptive Explanations of Programming Errors. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20896

article_title: Navigating the skill diversity frontier: How skill complexity explains worker resilience
citation: Carpanelli, M., Duszynski, J. & Stephany, F. (2026). Navigating the skill diversity frontier: How skill complexity explains worker resilience. Working paper, Oxford Internet Institute. https://oii.ox.ac.uk
title: Skill complexity framework: productive capital, adaptive capital, and the diversity frontier
description: The framework models human capital as a structured skill system rather than a list of attributes. It decomposes portfolios into productive capital, defined as "the market value associated with specialised expertise", and adaptive capital, "the flexibility generated by spanning multiple skill domains". It further postulates that specialisation constrains attainable diversity, yielding the diversity frontier: an inverse U-shaped upper envelope of diversity given specialisation. Workers on the frontier combine domain-specific expertise with cross-domain capabilities and are expected to be best positioned to learn, move, and adapt to technological change.
requirements: A directed skill network reconstructed from observed skill co-occurrence, with hierarchy inferred from asymmetric conditional probabilities and domains identified via community detection
constraints: The analysis remains associational rather than causal, despite the use of lagged explanatory variables and extensive controls
LinkedIn profiles over-represent digitally engaged and highly skilled occupations, and listed skills are self-reported
target_learners: Adult workers in knowledge-intensive labour markets facing technological change
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of new and AI-relevant skills
Occupational mobility and reskilling pathway identification
examples: The study operationalises the framework with specialisation as average inverse normalised local reaching centrality, diversity as Hill diversity across 12 Louvain skill domains, and a frontier score ranging from 0 to 1 within 100 specialisation groups
key_sources: Carpanelli, M., Duszynski, J. & Stephany, F. (2026). Navigating the skill diversity frontier: How skill complexity explains worker resilience. Working paper, Oxford Internet Institute. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02102

article_title: Open Questions Towards Skill-Sustaining Reliance in Reflective AI Engagement
citation: Sander de Jong. (2026). Open Questions Towards Skill-Sustaining Reliance in Reflective AI Engagement. Workshop paper presented at CHIWORK'26 Workshop on Human Agency and Skill in AI-Supported Work. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27726
title: Skill-sustaining reliance: reflective AI engagement assessed for long-term sustainability of human agency and expertise
description: The paper introduces the concern of "skill-sustaining reliance": designing and evaluating reflective AI-engagement mechanisms not only for immediate decision quality but for whether professionals "still develop their own expertise or slowly lose the capacity for independent judgement". It organises the problem around four challenges: varying user effects, efficiency-driven workflows, habituation of scaffolding, and the short-term evidence gap. Its contribution is a set of open questions (Q1–Q4) for the research community about the conditions under which reflective AI engagement can be sustained in practice.
requirements: Evaluation must extend beyond single-session metrics such as task accuracy, reliance rate, and trust calibration to longitudinal outcomes of independent reasoning capacity.
constraints: The paper offers no empirical test of the framework; it explicitly frames its contributions as open questions, noting long-term evidence is currently insufficient.
target_learners: Professionals using AI decision support in high-stakes domains such as healthcare
target_learning_goals: Sustaining independent judgement and metacognitive capacity during long-term AI-assisted decision-making
examples: The paper's example of clinicians who routinely review AI-suggested diagnoses performing well in sessions while possibly not developing the diagnostic reasoning unassisted practice would have demanded.
key_sources: Sander de Jong. (2026). Open Questions Towards Skill-Sustaining Reliance in Reflective AI Engagement. Workshop paper presented at CHIWORK'26 Workshop on Human Agency and Skill in AI-Supported Work. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27726

article_title: BEYOND EXPLICIT RULE LEARNING
citation: Robert M. DeKeyser. (1997). Beyond Explicit Rule Learning: Automatizing Second Language Morphosyntax. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 19, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263197002040
title: Skill acquisition theory accounts for L2 morphosyntactic automatization
description: The article interprets its findings within current skill acquisition theory, the framework holding that cognitive skills — including second language morphosyntactic skills — are acquired through practice and become automatized gradually. The study's results are presented as support: skill-specific learning and power-function improvement over 8 weeks of practice match the theory's predictions for other cognitive skills. The author states the results "are consistent with current skill acquisition theory."
requirements: Learners must first reach criterion on metalinguistic tests of the rules before systematic practice toward automatization
constraints: Evidence comes from taught rules in an artificial language practiced under computer-controlled conditions
target_learners: adult second language learners in a controlled experimental setting
target_learning_goals: automatization of explicitly learned L2 morphosyntactic rules in comprehension and production
examples: 61 subjects were taught four morphosyntactic rules and 32 vocabulary items in an artificial language, then practiced them for 8 weeks in computer-controlled comprehension and production tasks
key_sources: Robert M. DeKeyser. (1997). Beyond Explicit Rule Learning: Automatizing Second Language Morphosyntax. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 19, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263197002040

article_title: AI literacy and its implications for prompt engineering strategies
citation: Knoth, N., Tolzin, A., Janson, A., & Leimeister, J. M. (2024). AI literacy and its implications for prompt engineering strategies. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2024.100225
title: Skill-based approach to prompt engineering for non-expert users of LLM-based AI systems
description: The article introduces a skill-based approach to prompt engineering, treating the formulation of instructions to LLMs as a learnable skill rather than an ad hoc activity. Prompt engineering is defined as "a skill of formulating precise and well-structured instructions to elicit desired responses or information from the LLM, optimizing the effectiveness of the interaction". The approach is applied to non-expert users, specifically students in higher education, and is linked empirically to output quality and AI literacy.
requirements: Users must interact with LLM-based AI systems in a goal-directed manner for prompt engineering to function as a skill
constraints: Research on non-expert perspectives and on how AI literacy affects prompting behavior is described as lacking
target_learners: higher education students
non-expert users of LLM-based AI systems
target_learning_goals: formulating precise and well-structured instructions to LLMs
effective goal-directed use of generative AI tools
examples: The study examined students' intuitive behaviors towards LLM-based AI systems and linked prompt engineering skill quality to LLM output quality
key_sources: Knoth, N., Tolzin, A., Janson, A., & Leimeister, J. M. (2024). AI literacy and its implications for prompt engineering strategies. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2024.100225

article_title: The costs and benefits of providing feedback during learning
citation: Matthew Jensen Hays, Nate Kornell, and Robert A. Bjork. (2010). The costs and benefits of providing feedback during learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review. https://doi.org/10.3758/PBR.17.6.797
title: When study time is fixed, skip feedback after successful retrieval in favor of additional retrieval attempts
description: This principle holds that under a constrained time budget, presenting feedback after an already-successful retrieval wastes time that could fund further retrieval practice, which benefits memory more. The article's experiment showed that "skipping a feedback trial allowed time for an additional trial," and that final recall was higher when skipping was permitted. The authors state that "providing feedback is not universally beneficial" and can have "a negative net effect on learning."
requirements: Learners or the system must be able to judge or guess response correctness so feedback is skipped mainly after successful retrievals
Total learning time must be constrained, so time saved converts into additional retrieval trials
constraints: Feedback remains beneficial after incorrect responses and after correct responses made with low confidence or when feedback is delayed
Learners are typically unaware that retrieval outperforms restudy, so unguided skipping may be nonoptimal in other paradigms
target_learners: adult learners studying paired-associate material such as vocabulary flash cards
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of verbal, vocabulary, or factual material
examples: In the experiment, the computer skipped feedback after correct responses to make room for more test trials, and participants who skipped feedback themselves recalled more on the 24–48-hour delayed final test
key_sources: Matthew Jensen Hays, Nate Kornell, and Robert A. Bjork. (2010). The costs and benefits of providing feedback during learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review. https://doi.org/10.3758/PBR.17.6.797

article_title: Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues
citation: Baruch B. Schwarz, Udi Tsemach, Mirit Israeli, Erez Nir. (2025). Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09669-5
title: Skidmore's dialogic sphere: three dimensions of addressivity, voicing, and semantic permeability
description: The article presents Skidmore's framework, which extends the concept of dialogic space using Bakhtin's social theory of language, as a dialogic sphere with three dimensions. "First, addressivity materializes the fact that in a speech there is always a kind of interlocutor, the quality of turning to someone". The second dimension is the voicing given to students, contrasting teacher-orchestrated homophonic plenary talk with student voice. The third, semantic permeability, varies between heteroglossic everyday speech and orthoglossic academic language, requiring enough permeability for students to cross between them.
requirements: Judging whether teacher orientation toward learners is appropriate depends on the specific context in which the talk takes place
constraints: The framework makes salient the tension between dialogism (dialogic by definition) and Dialogic Education (dialogic because appropriate educational aims are reached in situ)
target_learners: Classroom students in dialogic education settings
target_learning_goals: Participation in educational dialogues bridging everyday and academic understanding
examples: The researchers used the three dimensions while watching and listening to all recorded discussions to select episodes exemplifying (in-)appropriate orientation
key_sources: Baruch B. Schwarz, Udi Tsemach, Mirit Israeli, Erez Nir. (2025). Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09669-5

article_title: Knowing how to learn: development and validation of the strategy knowledge test for self-regulated learning (SKT-SRL) for college students
citation: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Jörn R. Sparfeldt, Franziska Perels. (2024). Knowing how to learn: development and validation of the strategy knowledge test for self-regulated learning (SKT-SRL) for college students. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09379-w
title: SKT-SRL: a scenario-based conditional strategy knowledge test for college students
description: The SKT-SRL is a scenario-based offline instrument assessing conditional SRL strategy knowledge, defined as knowledge about which strategy is most useful for a specific learning situation. It presents seven learning scenarios, each with three useful and three less useful strategies, and scores learners on how well they differentiate useful from less useful strategies. It is the first test combining cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational components within a process model viewpoint for college students.
requirements: Requires expert ratings to establish scoring standards for useful versus less useful strategies per scenario
constraints: Developed and validated with German-speaking college students in Germany
target_learners: college students
target_learning_goals: conditional self-regulated learning strategy knowledge across cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational components
examples: Seven scenarios covering planning, performance, and reflection phases; students rate six strategies per scenario on a four-point Likert scale
key_sources: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Jörn R. Sparfeldt, Franziska Perels. (2024). Knowing how to learn: development and validation of the strategy knowledge test for self-regulated learning (SKT-SRL) for college students. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09379-w

article_title: Relations between undergraduates’ self-regulated learning skill mastery during digital training and biology performance
citation: Matthew L. Bernacki, Megan Claire Cogliano, Shelbi L. Kuhlmann, Jenifer Utz, Christy Strong, Jonathan C. Hilpert, Jeffrey A. Greene. (2023). Relations between undergraduates’ self-regulated learning skill mastery during digital training and biology performance. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09356-9
title: Skill-training design model: introduce surface declarative knowledge, consolidate to conceptual understanding, then prepare transfer to applied settings
description: The article organizes its training design and analyses around models of learning-skill development, chiefly Hattie and Donoghue's (2016) framework and Efklides' (2011) MASRL model. These hold that trainings "should introduce surface-level declarative knowledge about a skill and consolidate that knowledge to a conceptual level of understanding," and should include "activities that promote transfer" so learners can apply skills in authentic settings. Metacognitive knowledge of skills accrues from metacognitive experiences. The studies test whether mastery at each depth predicts later course performance.
requirements: Training must provide exposure and opportunities to engage in SRL so learners develop metacognitive knowledge of skills
Activities must assess declarative, conceptual, and applied knowledge of the skills
constraints: The article notes meta-analyses' moderator analyses "provide little information as to why such programs are effective"
target_learners: Undergraduate students in high-enrollment STEM gateway courses
target_learning_goals: Declarative, conceptual, and applied biology learning objectives
Self-regulated learning skills including cognitive strategies and regulation of behavior and environment
examples: The Science of Learning to Learn training introduced skills via direct instruction (definitions, theory, evidence), then had students rehearse and demonstrate declarative and conceptual knowledge and complete hypothetical planning activities applying skills to their course
key_sources: Matthew L. Bernacki, Megan Claire Cogliano, Shelbi L. Kuhlmann, Jenifer Utz, Christy Strong, Jonathan C. Hilpert, Jeffrey A. Greene. (2023). Relations between undergraduates’ self-regulated learning skill mastery during digital training and biology performance. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09356-9

article_title: Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science
citation: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9
title: Skinner's system approach: four guideposts (motivational resilience, academic identity, complex social ecologies, developmental embeddedness) for principled motivational integration
description: In the special issue's final paper, Skinner advances a 'system approach' in which all theories describe parts of a larger motivational system. Integration begins by identifying 'big ideas' common to the field. She proposes four guideposts: motivational resilience covering 'the energy, direction, and durability of action'; academic identity covering self-system processes; complex social ecologies incorporating classroom and meso-/macro-environmental factors; and developmental embeddedness. She locates constructs from different theories within this system and gives teachers concrete recommendations.
requirements: Integration should proceed by identifying common 'big ideas' rather than merging constructs wholesale
constraints: The essay presents this as one paper's proposal within the special issue, not a field consensus
target_learners: motivation researchers
teachers and practitioners
target_learning_goals: locating motivational theories within a common system to improve teaching and learning
examples: Skinner provides specific examples of how different motivational theories and constructs can be located within the larger motivational system
key_sources: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9

Testing the Impact of a Skill-Targeted Social and Emotional Learning Curriculum and its Variation by Pre- and Post-Migration Conflict Experiences: A Cluster Randomized Trial with Syrian Refugee Children in Lebanon.

The curriculum is the intervention whose impact is tested in "A Cluster Randomized Trial with Syrian Refugee Children in Lebanon". article_title: Through the Telescope: A Systematic Review of Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Their Applications in Psychomotor Skill Learning
citation: Gianluca Romano, Jan Schneider, Daniele Di Mitri, Hendrik Drachsler. (2025). Through the Telescope: A Systematic Review of Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Their Applications in Psychomotor Skill Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00526-1
title: The skill continua framework as a one-dimensional classification of psychomotor skill types
description: Davis et al. (2000) and Galligan et al. (2000) classify skills on six continua: "Granularity (fine-gross), Environment (open-close), Pace (internally-externally), Continuity (discrete-serial-continuous), Interactivity (individual-coactive-interactive) and Complexity (simple-complex)". The review prefers this one-dimensional framework over Gentile's two-dimensional 16-class taxonomy because its simplicity mitigates interpretation errors that could distort the picture of the ITS landscape, while still providing a good overview of the skill types ITS were developed for.
requirements: A classification framework is required because the type of skill influences the implementation of an ITS
constraints: The framework is one-dimensional, so unlike Gentile's taxonomy it does not provide a deeper view of pacing and environmental aspects including inertial variability and object manipulation
target_learners: Designers and researchers classifying psychomotor skills for ITS development
target_learning_goals: Understanding how skill type shapes psychomotor skill training
examples: The review classifies basic surgical tasks (pulling, grasping, navigating) as internally paced, closed, discrete, and individual, with advanced procedures as externally paced and serial
key_sources: Gianluca Romano, Jan Schneider, Daniele Di Mitri, Hendrik Drachsler. (2025). Through the Telescope: A Systematic Review of Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Their Applications in Psychomotor Skill Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00526-1

article_title: Designing for robot-mediated interaction among culturally and linguistically diverse children
citation: Yanghee Kim, Sherry Marx, Hung Viet Pham, Tung Nguyen. (2021). Designing for robot-mediated interaction among culturally and linguistically diverse children. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10051-2
title: Skusie: a bilingual humanoid social robot system with wizard-of-Oz control
description: Skusie was a humanoid social robot used to mediate collaborative interactions among kindergarten pairs. The robotic system included four components: the robot, a robot controller app on an Android phone in its head serving as its display screen, a main controller app on a separate Android tablet used for Wizard-of-Oz control, and an FTP-based file server storing code, scripts, image data, and interaction logs. The robot was bilingual in Spanish and English and displayed photos on its smartphone brain during activities.
requirements: A researcher wizard controlling the robot's speech and movements from a discrete location in the room
constraints: Skusie's utterances were limited and imperfect, and natural dialogue was not possible because natural language processing and automatic speech recognition for children is still developing
target_learners: culturally and linguistically diverse kindergarten children
target_learning_goals: collaborative interaction and peer play
examples: Skusie displayed a photo of a penguin and asked the children, "Is this an animal?"
key_sources: Yanghee Kim, Sherry Marx, Hung Viet Pham, Tung Nguyen. (2021). Designing for robot-mediated interaction among culturally and linguistically diverse children. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10051-2

article_title: Death of the paediatric manikin: a scoping review.
citation: Apara Teleireoluwa, Hogan Tom, Peterson Jennifer L H. (2024). Death of the paediatric manikin: a scoping review. BMJ Paediatrics Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjpo-2024-002941
title: Debriefs after paediatric manikin death need skilled facilitation with designated time for emotional and communication discussion
description: The review concludes that the debrief has a crucial role in mitigating potentially negative impacts of paediatric manikin death. From the qualitative participant data, it would seem preferable for facilitators to use a debrief incorporating "designated time and space for discussion of the emotional and communication elements of the simulation scenario", while maintaining psychological safety through clear discouragement of blame. Facilitators should state at the debrief's start when death was a predetermined learning objective.
requirements: Experienced facilitators are needed to manage debriefs while maintaining psychological safety
Learning objectives for the scenario should be clearly articulated in the debrief
constraints: No specific debriefing model was evaluated in the included studies; the recommendation derives from qualitative participant data
target_learners: qualified paediatric doctors
paediatric nurses
target_learning_goals: processing emotional responses to patient death
reflecting on team resuscitation performance
examples: In the included studies, facilitator reassurance that death was a learning objective plus a facilitated debrief allowed participants to work through their discomfort
key_sources: Apara Teleireoluwa, Hogan Tom, Peterson Jennifer L H. (2024). Death of the paediatric manikin: a scoping review. BMJ Paediatrics Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjpo-2024-002941

article_title: Improving Oral and Written Narration and Reading Comprehension of Children At-Risk for Language and Literacy Difficulties: Results of a Randomized Clinical Trial
citation: Gillam, S. L., Vaughn, S., Roberts, G., Capin, P., Fall, A.-M., Israelsen-Augenstein, M., Holbrook, S., Wada, R., Hancock, A., Fox, C., Dille, J., Magimairaj, B. M., & Gillam, R. B. (2022). Improving Oral and Written Narration and Reading Comprehension of Children at-Risk for Language and Literacy Difficulties: Results of a Randomized Clinical Trial. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000766
title: SKILL's theoretical grounding: ACT-R, the Embedded Processes model of working memory, and the Construction-Integration model
description: The SKILL program was designed from three cognitive models of how information is stored, activated, and used in comprehension and production: the Adaptive Control of Thought (ACT-R) model, the Embedded Processes model of working memory, and the Construction-Integration (CI) model. In all three, discourse comprehension and production are multilevel processes drawing on object, event, and language knowledge in associative networks in long-term memory. ACT-R frames story structure knowledge as "chunks" that "become increasingly large and complex as a function of experience listening to and telling more complex stories"; the CI model describes integration into a situation model. The three phases of SKILL were designed to transfer this orientation into learning activities building organizational frameworks in episodic memory.
requirements: Instruction must move students through the three phases: teaching story structure and causal language, strategies for creating a situation model, and strategies for integration into long-term memory.
constraints: The article states the models are theoretical underpinnings; it does not test the models themselves.
target_learners: Elementary students in Grades 1–4 at risk for language and literacy difficulties
target_learning_goals: Oral narrative comprehension and production
Written narration
Literate language and story grammar knowledge
examples: Phase I uses verbal and visual cues, wordless picture books, and graphic organizers to build complete single-episode stories; Phase III has students create and retell multi-episodic stories using a rubric of macrostructure and microstructure features.
key_sources: Gillam, S. L., Vaughn, S., Roberts, G., Capin, P., Fall, A.-M., Israelsen-Augenstein, M., Holbrook, S., Wada, R., Hancock, A., Fox, C., Dille, J., Magimairaj, B. M., & Gillam, R. B. article_title: The Effect of Speed Reading Strategies on Developing Reading Comprehension among the 2nd Secondary Students in English Language
citation: Mahmoud Sulaiman Hamad Bani Abdelrahman & Muwafaq Saleem Bsharah. (2014). The Effect of Speed Reading Strategies on Developing Reading Comprehension among the 2nd Secondary Students in English Language. English Language Teaching, 7(6). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n6p168
title: Skimming and scanning as the two core speed reading strategies
description: The article presents skimming and scanning as the two speed reading strategies at the core of its training material. Skimming is "reading a text or a passage quickly to get a general idea", done without reading every word, using the title, introduction, headings, pictures and summary. Scanning is "to cover a great deal of material rapidly to locate a specific facet or pi ece of information", useful for finding a specific name, date, statistic or fact without reading the whole text. The article cites Brown (1994) calling them "perhaps the two most valuable reading strategies for learners as well as native speakers".
requirements: Learners need practice in both strategies; the article states that to be fast in comprehending a text, the learner needs to practice skimming and scanning.
constraints: Pugh (1978) is cited suggesting scanning, being a less complex style of reading, can be introduced first, while skimming requires greater fluency and more practice so should be introduced later.
target_learners: second secondary literary stream students learning English in Jordan
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
reading speed
locating specific information in texts
examples: The study's training material, adapted from Rababa'h (1991), trained the experimental section on these two strategies during the first semester of 2013/2014.

article_title: Sketch Strategy of Knowledge in Physics Learning and Its Influence on Metacognitive
citation: Bunga D. Amin, Helmi Abdullah and Jasruddin D. Malago. (2018). Sketch strategy of knowledge in physics learning and its influence on metacognitive. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2017.3293
title: Sketch knowledge strategy (SKS): a three-stage procedure of Making, Formulating and Executing
description: The article defines sketch knowledge strategy as "a procedure in physics questions that consists of three stages": Making, Formulating and Executing. Making visualizes the question statement and pours it into a sketch completed with the given quantities; Formulating uses principles, laws and basic formulas to frame equations based on the sketch; Executing applies mathematical principles to determine the requested parameter. The article contrasts SKS with the target variable strategy, whose weakness it locates in the stage of translating the problem statement.
requirements: Students must translate verbal problem statements into sketches filled with quantities, concepts and principles of physics
target_learners: physics education graduate students
high school physics students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive knowledge (factual, conceptual, procedural)
higher order thinking in physics problem solving
examples: In the quasi-experiment, class-A was taught Mechanics topics (straight motion with constant acceleration, parabolic motion, force and motion) using SKS while class-B used TVS

article_title: Rapid skill acquisition through task-specific ultrasound training for peripheral cannulation in medical students.
citation: Lin Xu-Nian, Lu Cheng-Wei, Lin Tzu-Yu, Chou San-Fang, Chang Ya-Ying. (2026). Rapid skill acquisition through task-specific ultrasound training for peripheral cannulation in medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09935-9
title: Skill-focused curriculum design: task-specific modifications to reduce cognitive load and target a single procedural objective
description: The article modified a comprehensive anesthesiology resident curriculum into a skill-focused version targeting one objective: successful US-guided cannulation. Key modifications included removing US physics content "in order to shorten the training duration and reduce cognitive load", using only large-gauge (16G) needles, teaching only the out-of-plane approach with DNTP, and activating an on-screen midline guidance indicator. Table 1 contrasts the two curricula across goal, content scope, duration, cognitive load, teaching context, outcome, and educational efficiency dimensions.
requirements: A simulation model and handheld US device with an on-screen midline guidance indicator are needed to implement the curriculum as described.
constraints: The curriculum exclusively emphasizes the out-of-plane approach with DNTP and large-gauge needles, which "may not reflect typical clinical practice".
target_learners: Undergraduate medical clerks
Postgraduate year (PGY) residents
target_learning_goals: US-guided peripheral intravenous cannulation
Needle tip visualization under ultrasound
examples: The 25-min session comprised a 10-min instructional video, a 5-min live demonstration, and 10 min of supervised self-practice on a Blue Phantom model.

article_title: Cumulative access to print books improves literacy achievement: Evidence from a five-year randomized trial in high-poverty schools.
citation: Borman Geoffrey D., Yang Hyunwoo. (2026). Cumulative access to print books improves literacy achievement: Evidence from a five-year randomized trial in high-poverty schools. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2521416123
title: Skill-development theory: access to books directly improves literacy through increased print exposure and reading practice
description: Skill-development theory holds that "greater access to books directly improves literacy through increased print exposure and reading practice," contrasting with the cultural capital account in which home libraries merely proxy broader family resources. The article's theory of action posits that sustained access to high-interest, culturally relevant books strengthens the home literacy environment, increases voluntary reading and print exposure, and improves achievement, with effects accumulating through recursive Matthew effects and moderated by baseline context. The trial's causal results are presented as evidence supporting this theory.
requirements: Sustained, cumulative access to books over multiple years; the article states impacts depended on cumulative and sustained exposure
constraints: The article did not measure changes in the home literacy environment, books actually read, self-efficacy, or how theorized Matthew effects evolved
target_learners: Elementary students (grades 1-2 at baseline) in high-poverty urban schools
target_learning_goals: Reading achievement and literacy development
examples: The five-year cluster-randomized trial in 60 Milwaukee elementary schools tested the theory by providing up to 34 books per student while withholding books in control schools

Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2521416123

article_title: Skinner's programmed instruction improves diabetes knowledge and skills of undergraduate nursing students: a randomised controlled trial.
citation: Zhang Ying, Zhang Yixuan, Wang Xiaofang, Luo Baoping. (2026). Skinner's programmed instruction improves diabetes knowledge and skills of undergraduate nursing students: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09031-y
title: Skinner's programmed instruction model: five principles for sequenced, feedback-driven learning
description: The article applies Skinner's programmed instruction as an explanatory and design framework for clinical nursing education. It states that "Skinner's programmed instruction model emphasises five principles: small steps, active responding, immediate feedback, self-pacing, and student evaluation (low error rate)". Content is broken into manageable units sequenced from simple to complex, learners progress at their own pace, errors are minimised to protect motivation, and immediate feedback consolidates correct responses. The trial operationalised these principles with QR-code micro-videos, Bluetooth vibration feedback, model rollback, and electronic heatmaps.
requirements: Content must be segmented into small, logically sequenced modules arranged by increasing difficulty
Immediate feedback mechanisms must be available so errors are corrected as they arise
Clinical instructors require targeted training in the principles and application methods
constraints: The authors note the behaviourist framework does not fully capture critical thinking and empathy, which are key nursing competencies
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students in clinical placements
target_learning_goals: diabetes-related declarative knowledge
psychomotor clinical skills such as insulin injection and blood glucose monitoring
self-efficacy
examples: The experimental intervention translated the five principles into QR-code micro-videos, Bluetooth vibration for instant feedback, model rollback, and electronic heatmaps over a 4-week, 60-class-hour block
key_sources: Zhang Ying, Zhang Yixuan, Wang Xiaofang, Luo Baoping. (2026). Skinner's programmed instruction improves diabetes knowledge and skills of undergraduate nursing students: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09031-y

article_title: "Script Killing" immersive teaching improves the competency of emergency medicine residents rotating across departments.
citation: Zhang Dalong, Gao Jiankai, Niu Xingguo, Si Haoran, Sun Yang, Li Mingzhe, Yao Tianyi, Tang Juhua. (2026). "Script Killing" immersive teaching improves the competency of emergency medicine residents rotating across departments. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1806065
title: Script Killing Immersive Teaching (SKIT) model: full-process task chain, role responsibility binding, and dynamic NPC intervention
description: SKIT is a murder-mystery game–based, role-play scenario simulation approach in which rotating residents play patients, family members, doctors, and nurses under instructor guidance. The article describes three core mechanisms: "a full-process task chain (pre-hospital-in-hospital-ward full cycle), role responsibility binding (clear division of labor to avoid bystander effect), and dynamic variable intervention (NPC creates real conflicts)". Scripts are written by experienced teaching physicians and release key information in stages contingent on learner actions, with debriefing after play.

Instructor guidance for dynamic intervention and debriefing
Role assignment with clearly defined hierarchical tasks
constraints: Does not address technical procedural skills, per the authors' limitations
Implemented over a 3-month emergency rotation in this study
target_learners: Non-emergency resident physicians rotating through the emergency department
target_learning_goals: Emergency clinical decision-making
Interprofessional teamwork and communication
Triage and disposition planning
examples: Box 1 example scenario: traffic accident with suspected traumatic brain injury, three timed decision checkpoints, and SBAR/ISBAR-style handoff outputs

article_title: Health science staff and student experiences of teaching and assessing clinical skills using digital tools: a qualitative study.
citation: O’Brien A, Forde C. (2023). Health science staff and student experiences of teaching and assessing clinical skills using digital tools: a qualitative study. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2023.2256656
title: Skill layering: use digital tools to support the 'see one' and 'do one' layers of multifaceted clinical skills
description: Participants described clinical competencies as multi-layered and multifaceted, with individual low-stake component skills teachable online while holistic integrated application requires clinical settings. The article frames skill learning as a layering process in which technology can enhance the demonstration layer of pre-recorded demonstrations and the practice layer of simulations allowing mistakes, while deeper layers need in-person work.
requirements: Identify which layers of a skill (e.g. visual, auditory, haptic) can be supported by technology
constraints: Integrated application of multiple skills simultaneously, such as clinical reasoning, was reported as difficult to teach remotely
target_learners: health science students
health science educators
target_learning_goals: practical clinical skill acquisition and competency
examples: Staff took time to ensure pre-recorded demonstrations were of high quality and students practised skills in simulations where mistakes were permitted

article_title: E-Learning Material of Evidence-Based Medicine for Laypersons.
citation: Okabayashi, S., Kitazawa, K., Kawamura, T., & Nakayama, T. (2022). E-Learning Material of Evidence-Based Medicine for Laypersons. HLRP: Health Literacy Research and Practice, 6(4), e290-e299. https://doi.org/10.3928/24748307-20221113-01
title: Programmed-learning design pattern: active true/false response, immediate feedback, small steps, self-pacing, and learner verification
description: The material applies Skinner's (1968) five principles of programmed learning as its instructional pattern: learners actively answer true/false quizzes, receive immediate feedback with explanations, progress through small steps, learn at their own pace by returning to earlier material, and the program's value is verified by trials with learners lacking subject knowledge. "This study adopted true/false quizzes, and the users were required to select their answer actively." An optional page lets learners study more if they desire.
requirements: Learners with no knowledge of the subject matter must try the program under development so the material can be improved based on the trials
constraints: The gaming procedure used was simple, such as true/false quizzes and scoring correct answers
target_learners: Adult laypersons without prior EBM knowledge
target_learning_goals: Understanding essential components of EBM and epidemiology for everyday health decisions
examples: True/false quizzes created for each element with correct answers and explanations shown immediately after answering, and pages turned like a book

article_title: The Effects of Adolescent Childbearing on Literacy and Numeracy in Bangladesh, Malawi, and Zambia.
citation: Psaki Stephanie R., Soler-Hampejsek Erica, Saha Jyotirmoy, Mensch Barbara S., Amin Sajeda. (2019). The Effects of Adolescent Childbearing on Literacy and Numeracy in Bangladesh, Malawi, and Zambia. Demography. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13524-019-00816-z
title: Skill-retention threshold theory: passing the transition from learning to read to reading to learn protects academic skills against deterioration after school leaving
description: The article's organizing framework holds that academic skills may improve or deteriorate after school leaving "depending on whether they are reinforced through regular use". Drawing on Chall's stages of reading and the fourth grade slump, it proposes that four to six years of schooling form a foundation for lifelong literacy, so learners who made the transition to "reading to learn" retain skills, while those below the threshold lose skills permanently when changing roles prevent use. This theory motivates the hypothesized grade attainment × childbearing interaction.
requirements: Skills must be assessed repeatedly after school leaving to observe deterioration or retention
constraints: The article notes skills may improve or deteriorate depending on whether they are reinforced through regular use
target_learners: Adolescent girls in low- and middle-income countries transitioning from school to marriage and childbearing
target_learning_goals: Retention of literacy and numeracy skills gained in school after school leaving
examples: The study tests this theory by estimating interactions between first birth and grade attainment in fixed-effects models across three longitudinal samples
key_sources: Psaki Stephanie R., Soler-Hampejsek Erica, Saha Jyotirmoy, Mensch Barbara S., Amin Sajeda. (2019). The Effects of Adolescent Childbearing on Literacy and Numeracy in Bangladesh, Malawi, and Zambia. Demography. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13524-019-00816-z

progressive proficiency in minimally invasive procedures
